title: You need exactly-once across a database write and a Kafka publish: why don't Kafka transactions cover this, and what is the fix (transactional outbox)?
shortTitle: You need exactly-once across a database write and a Kafka publish: why don't Kafka transactions cover this, and what is the fix (transactional outbox)?

s1_definition.oneliner: Kafka transactions are atomic only within Kafka, so for atomicity across a database write and a Kafka publish you use the transactional outbox -- write the business row and an outbox row in one local DB transaction, then a relay publishes the outbox at least once with an idempotency key.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Kafka transaction scope** -- atomic across Kafka topic writes and consumer offset commits only; has no visibility into or control over external databases.
- **Dual-write problem** -- writing to both a database and Kafka cannot be made atomic because they have separate transaction managers with no shared coordinator.
- **Transactional outbox** -- in one local DB transaction, write the business row and an outbox row; a separate relay reads the outbox and publishes to Kafka.
- **At-least-once relay** -- the relay may republish on crash, so each outbox event carries a unique id for consumer-side dedup, giving end-to-end exactly-once effect.
- **Relay options** -- polling publisher (simple, DB-agnostic) or change data capture with Debezium (lower latency, decoupled from app code).
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India must do two things when Rajesh transfers money: update the ledger and send a notice to the clearing house. Kafka's all-or-nothing guarantee only covers the clearing house's internal paperwork. If the clerk updates the ledger and then the line to the clearing house drops, the two are out of sync. The outbox fix: in the same trip to the ledger, the clerk writes both the entry and a note in an outbox column. A separate messenger reads the outbox and sends the notice.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Kafka transactions are atomic only within Kafka; they cannot span an external database. The naive dual write -- database then Kafka or Kafka then database -- is unsafe in both orderings because a crash in the gap leaves the two systems out of sync.

The transactional outbox pattern solves this by removing the dual write. In one local database transaction, write both the business change and an outbox row. A relay reads unpublished rows and publishes to Kafka. Because delivery is at-least-once, consumers deduplicate using the outbox event id.

In my National Bank of India transfer service, we lost events from the dual write when the broker was briefly unreachable. The outbox fixed it: the database became the single source of truth, and the relay published with dedup keys for end-to-end exactly-once effect.

Remember one sentence: Kafka transactions give atomicity inside Kafka, and the transactional outbox gives atomicity between your database and Kafka by making the database the single source of truth.

---

keyPoints: Kafka transactions are atomic only within Kafka; they have no control over external databases.
The dual-write problem: writing to both a database and Kafka cannot be made atomic because they have separate transaction managers.
The transactional outbox writes the business row and an outbox row in one local DB transaction.
A relay (polling or CDC) reads the outbox and publishes to Kafka with at-least-once delivery.
Each outbox event carries a unique id for consumer-side dedup, giving end-to-end exactly-once effect.
CDC with Debezium tails the DB transaction log for lower latency and decoupled publishing.
